[META | FY2025 Q4 | TRANSCRIPT]
Speaker: Susan Li, CFO
The optimizations we made in Q4 drove a 20% lift in Threads time spent.

Turning to 2026, we see a lot of opportunity to drive additional gains.

This includes scaling the complexity and amount of training data we use in our models while continuing to make our systems more responsive to people’s real-time interests. We’re also focused on incorporating LLMs to understand content more deeply across our platform, which will enable more personalized recommendations.

Another big area of investment this year is developing the next generation of our recommendation systems. We have several big bets on this front, including building new model architectures from the ground up that will work on top of LLMs, leveraging the world knowledge and reasoning capabilities of an LLM to better infer people’s interests.

Beyond improvements to our recommendation systems, we expect to use the models developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs to deliver compelling and differentiated AI products.

One area we’re already seeing promise is with AI dubbing of videos into local languages. We are now supporting nine different languages, with hundreds of millions of people watching AI translated videos every day. This is already driving incremental time spent on Instagram and we plan to launch support for more languages over the course of this year.

We are also seeing strong traction with our media creation tools. Nearly 10% of the Reels people view each day are now created in our Edits app, almost tripling from last quarter. Within Meta AI, the number of daily actives generating media tripled year-over-year in Q4. This year, we expect to advance the capabilities of our underlying media generation models and ship new features to further enhance the product experience.

Another area we’re focused on for Meta AI is personalization. We’re seeing in our early testing that personalized responses drive higher levels of engagement, and we expect to significantly advance the personalization of Meta AI this year. This dovetails with our investments in content understanding, which will enable our systems to develop a deeper understanding of each person’s interests and preferences while also identifying the most relevant content across our platform to pull into responses.

Turning to the second driver of our revenue performance: increasing monetization efficiency.

The first part of this work is optimizing the level of ads within organic engagement.

Here, our focus remains on tuning our systems to identify the right time and place to deliver ads. In some cases, this enables us to grow the overall level of ad load while preserving the user

experience. However, an increasingly important part of this work is finding opportunities to drive incremental conversions within the same overall level of ad load by determining when a person is more interested in seeing an ad. In fact, in the second half of 2025, our initiatives on Facebook to redistribute ads across users and sessions delivered a nearly 4x larger revenue impact than Facebook ad load increases.

[META | FY2026 Q3 | TRANSCRIPT]
Speaker: Susan Li, CFO
Meta One is rolling out gradually with more than 50

features across Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp, including Meta Business Agent and Meta AI, and has surpassed 15 million subscriptions and trials to date. The core experience across our apps and Meta AI will remain free, while subscriptions offer more specialized capabilities and expanded AI usage.

Beyond monetizing engagement across our existing services, we are building new experiences and revenue streams around consumer agents.

Mark highlighted the impressive early momentum with Muse. Users have found many reasons to use Muse with the top 3 categories being shopping, personal productivity and creativity. We are encouraged by the breadth of use cases, with shopping in particular being used by over 25% of Muse weekly actives.

While our near-term priority is to grow adoption and expand Muse's reach, we see multiple paths to monetization, beginning with subscriptions.

We also see a significant opportunity to extend Muse to small businesses. Based on a recent user survey, we estimate that at least 500 million self-identified small businesses use Meta's family of apps to reach customers and generate revenue. Muse could help these businesses acquire customers and operate more efficiently, while helping people complete transactions. Over time, consumer and business agents could connect and transact directly, creating opportunities around paid usage, commerce, and business services.

Alongside growth, we are focused on building sustainable unit economics. Muse's compute intensity means that expanding its user base will require significant investment, and we expect total serving costs to rise. At the same time, we expect to improve compute cost efficiency by more than tenfold over the next year, driven by better utilization of off-peak capacity, more efficient models and inference optimization.

As revenue scales, these efficiency gains give us confidence in our ability to build a highly profitable business over time.

Moving now to our financial outlook.

We expect fourth quarter 2026 total revenue to be in the range of $73-76 billion. Our guidance assumes foreign currency is an approximately 1% headwind to year-over-year total revenue growth, based on current exchange rates.

Turning to the expense and capex outlooks.

We are raising our expense outlook to incorporate the $9.9 billion charge related to legal proceedings recognized in Q3. We now expect full year 2026 total expenses to be in the range of $175-179 billion.

Excluding the Q3 legal charge, we continue to expect 2026 operating income to be above 2025 operating income.

At a segment level, we now expect Reality Labs losses to decline compared to 2025 to a range of $18-19 billion.

We anticipate 2026 capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, to be in the range of $135-145 billion, narrowed from our prior outlook of $130-145 billion.

Section: Cost of Revenue and Operating Expenses
Cost of revenue. Our cost of revenue consists of expenses associated with the delivery and distribution of our products. These mainly include infrastructure expenses related to the operation of our data centers and technical infrastructure, such as depreciation expense from servers, network infrastructure and buildings, employee compensation which includes payroll, share-based compensation and benefits for employees on our operations teams, energy and bandwidth costs, as well as third-party cloud costs. Cost of revenue also consists of processing fees and traffic acquisition costs, which include credit card and other fees related to processing customer transactions; RL inventory costs, which consist of cost of products sold and estimated losses on non-cancelable contractual commitments; and content and creator costs, which include payments to content creators from whom we license content for distribution, as well as incentive payments made to creators based on engagement.

Research and development. Research and development expenses consist mostly of employee compensation, which includes payroll, share-based compensation and benefits for our employees on our engineering and technical teams who are responsible for developing new technologies and products. Research and development expenses also include infrastructure expenses related to our data centers, technical infrastructure, and third-party cloud services; third-party AI token costs; RL technology development costs; and facilities-related costs.

Marketing and sales. Marketing and sales expenses consist mostly of employee compensation which includes payroll, share-based compensation and benefits for our employees engaged in sales, sales support, marketing, business development, and customer service functions; marketing and promotional expenses; professional services to support our community and product operations; and third-party AI token costs.

General and administrative. General and administrative expenses consist primarily of employee compensation which includes payroll, share-based compensation and benefits for certain of our executives as well as our legal, finance, human resources, corporate communications and policy, and other administrative employees; legal-related costs, which include

estimated fines, settlements, or other losses in connection with legal and related matters, as well as other legal fees; other taxes, such as digital services taxes and other non-income-based tax levies; and professional services.

Section: Legal and Related Matters
We filed a petition for a writ of certiorari with the U.S. Supreme Court on October 2, 2024, which was denied. We then moved to compel arbitration, which the district court denied. We appealed the denial of our motion to compel arbitration to the Ninth Circuit on December 3, 2025. The matter is stayed in district court pending resolution of our appeal.

Beginning on July 7, 2023, multiple cases, including putative class actions, were filed against us in the United States and elsewhere, alleging that we improperly acquired, distributed, and used various copyrighted materials and/or other types of data to train our artificial intelligence models and seeking unspecified damages and injunctive relief. In the United States, statutory damages for copyright liability are calculated on a per work basis, which may result in substantial damages, particularly given the large volumes of data required to train AI models. The cases in the United States, which were filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California (Kadrey, et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., Chabon, et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc. and Farnsworth v. Meta Platforms, Inc.) and U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York (Huckabee, et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc. et al., which was subsequently transferred to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California), have been consolidated into Kadrey, et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc. Motions for summary judgment were heard in this case on May 1, 2025, including on the issue of the applicability of the fair use defense to use of copyrighted books for generative AI model training. On June 25, 2025, the court granted our motion for summary judgment on fair use as to the named plaintiffs in the case. The parties will proceed to brief the remaining claims of copyright infringement and contributory infringement related to alleged distribution of books to third parties during the downloading process. The court is scheduled to hear summary judgment motions on February 25, 2027. Beginning in November 2025, additional cases with similar claims were filed against us in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California and the Southern District of New York (Entrepreneur Media v. Meta Platforms, Inc., Carreyrou et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., TED Entertainment, Inc. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., Chicken Soup for the Soul LLC v. Meta Platforms, Inc., Beaulier v. Section: Executive Overview of Third Quarter Results
Our mission is to build the future of human connection and the technology that makes it possible.

Our financial results and key Family metrics for the third quarter of 2026 are set forth below. Total revenue for the third quarter of 2026 was $64.60 billion, an increase of 26% compared to the third quarter of 2025, due to an increase in advertising revenue. [META | FY2026 Q3 | PRESS_RELEASE]
Section: CFO Outlook Commentary
We expect fourth quarter 2026 total revenue to be in the range of $73-76 billion. Our guidance assumes foreign currency is an approximately 1% headwind to year-over-year total revenue growth, based on current exchange rates.

We are raising our expense outlook to incorporate the $9.9 billion charge related to legal proceedings recognized in the third quarter. We now expect full year 2026 total expenses to be in the range of $175-179 billion.

Excluding the third quarter legal charge, we continue to expect 2026 operating income to be above 2025 operating income.

At a segment level, we now expect Reality Labs losses to decline compared to 2025 to a range of $18-19 billion.

We anticipate 2026 capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, to be in the range of $135-145 billion, narrowed from our prior outlook of $130-145 billion.

Absent any changes to our tax landscape, we expect our fourth quarter 2026 tax rate to be between 15-17%.

Additionally, we continue to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results. For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth-related issues in several markets and have a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the U.S.

Looking beyond 2026, we are still developing our budget and capacity plans for next year, but we expect to continue investing aggressively to support both our core business and emerging AI initiatives. Our current capacity and what is scheduled to come online gives us the flexibility to allocate resources across model training, core business growth, and the development and support of new products.

Our AI investments are already delivering substantial incremental advertising revenue through stronger engagement, better recommendations, and more efficient monetization. Building on this progress, our MSL investments are creating the technology and infrastructure needed to unlock significant new revenue opportunities and strengthen capabilities across the business. While these investments will take longer to generate returns than those in our core business, the breadth of monetization opportunities and internal efficiencies gives us confidence in their long-term potential.

Looking ahead, although we are not providing a full-year 2027 revenue outlook, the benefits our AI investments are delivering to the core business, combined with emerging opportunities from model advances and product launches, position us to sustain strong overall revenue growth throughout 2027.

Separately, we remain focused on improving Reality Labs profitability and expect losses to narrow next year to around $15 billion as we reallocate investment toward other priority areas, primarily AI.

Speaker: Susan Li, CFO
Thanks Mark and good afternoon everyone.

Let’s begin with our segment results. All comparisons are on a year-over-year basis unless otherwise noted.

Q3 Total Family of Apps revenue was $64.2 billion, up 26%.

Q3 Family of Apps ad revenue was $63.1 billion, up 26% on both a reported and constant currency basis.

In Q3, the total number of ad impressions served across our services increased 10%. Impression growth was healthy across all regions, driven by growth in engagement and users, as well as ad

load optimizations. The global average price per ad increased 14% year-over-year, driven by ad performance gains and improvements in macro conditions relative to Q3 of last year. This was partially offset by strong impression growth, particularly from lower-monetizing surfaces and regions.

Family of Apps other revenue was $1.1 billion and grew 59%, driven primarily by WhatsApp paid messaging and subscriptions revenue.

Within our Reality Labs segment, Q3 revenue was $443 million, down 6% due to lower Quest headset sales, which were partially offset by continued strong growth in AI glasses revenue.

Moving now to our consolidated results.

Q3 total revenue was $64.6 billion, up 26% on both a reported and constant currency basis.

Q3 total expenses were $51.6 billion, up 68% compared to last year, and included a $9.9 billion charge related to the August 2026 multistate attorneys general agreement. Year-over-year growth was primarily driven by legal-related costs, infrastructure costs, and third-party AI token costs.

The growth in infrastructure costs was driven by higher third party cloud spend, depreciation, and data center operating costs.

We ended Q3 with over 66,000 employees, down 12% from Q2 following the May 2026 headcount reduction.

Third quarter GAAP operating income was $13.0 billion, representing a 37% decline year-over- year and a 20% operating margin. Excluding the Q3 legal charges related to the aforementioned legal settlement, our third quarter operating income would have increased 11% year-over-year.

Our tax rate for the quarter was 24%, above our outlook range primarily driven by the non- deductible portion of legal expenses.

Net income was $9.9 billion or $3.83 per share.

Section: Legal and Related Matters
Although we are vigorously defending our regulatory compliance, we have accrued significant amounts for loss contingencies related to these inquiries and investigations in Europe, and we believe there is a reasonable possibility that additional accruals for losses related to

these matters could be material individually or in the aggregate. In addition, we are subject to individual and class actions in Europe relating to matters that are or have been the subject of regulatory investigations.

Beginning on June 7, 2021, multiple putative class actions were filed against us alleging that we improperly received individuals' information from third-party websites or apps via our business tools in violation of our terms and various state and federal laws and seeking unspecified damages and injunctive relief (for example, In re Meta Pixel Healthcare Litigation; In re Meta Pixel Tax Filing Cases; Frasco v. Flo Health, Inc.; Doe v. Hey Favor, Inc. et al.; Doe v. GoodRx Holdings, Inc. et al. in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California; and Rickwalder, et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc. in the Santa Clara County Superior Court). These cases are in different stages, but several of our motions to dismiss have been denied in whole or in part, while certain others have been granted in whole or in part. In Rickwalder, the Superior Court denied plaintiffs' motion for class certification and the plaintiffs have appealed that decision. In Meta Pixel Tax Filing Cases, on March 30, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California denied plaintiffs' motion for class certification. In Flo Health, on August 1, 2025, a jury returned a verdict on liability in favor of the plaintiffs and on behalf of a California subclass on the sole claim remaining against Meta under Section 632 of the California Invasion of Privacy Act. Plaintiffs are seeking $5,000 in statutory damages per class member and have asserted that there are up to approximately 1.25 million class members. The amount of potential damages is uncertain at this time. In addition, we are subject to individual and class actions in Europe and Canada, as well as regulatory investigations in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere, relating to similar matters with regard to our business tools.

Second quarter GAAP operating income was $18.8 billion, representing an 8% decline year-over- year and a 31% operating margin. Excluding the Q2 legal charges and severance expenses, our second quarter operating income would have increased 9% year-over-year.

Our tax rate for the quarter was 16%.

Net income was $15.8 billion or $6.18 per share.

[META | FY2026 Q3 | TRANSCRIPT]
Speaker: Mark Zuckerberg, CEO
Hey everyone. Thanks for joining today.

This has been a busy and exciting few months. Our family of apps is now used by 3.64 billion people each day, and we're seeing all-time highs in engagement on both Facebook and Instagram driven by strong growth in video. Threads has now overtaken X in monthly actives and continues to grow quickly. WhatsApp is hitting all-time highs in messaging and is becoming an increasingly important platform for agents as well.

In the last few months we have had several major milestones towards our goal of delivering personal superintelligence to everyone. We had one of our most successful launches ever with the Muse personal agent; we shipped Muse Wonder as our first frontier model; and we shipped several new glasses and gadgets with Muse integration, including coming soon to our new audio glasses.

We have been discussing our vision for personal superintelligence for more than a year now. We want to help every person have an extremely capable personal agent that understands your goals and can help you achieve them and improve your life in whatever ways you want -- whether that's improving your relationships, helping you save time, save money, build a business, create new things, or anything else that you can dream of. Muse is the product form of this vision. So now we have the foundational technology in place to deliver this. There is still a lot of work ahead, but our initial position is very strong.

In just a month and a half, more than 10 million people in the US and Canada have set up Muse personal agents. Growth continues to be strong and we have been #1 in the App Store almost every day. Engagement and retention are also off to a strong start. About 25% of people who have set up Muse use it on any given day. For our earliest adopters, the longer that they use Muse,

the better that retention seems to get. To put this in perspective, this is more than twice the level that Threads started at or where we believe that other AI apps started at as well.

The most common use case for Muse is shopping, with more than a quarter of people who are using Muse engaging in this with an average purchase size over $200. Plaid told us they hadn't seen activity like they're seeing with their connector on any other service before. And in the first week we had to work with Stripe to raise credit limits since the volumes were above what any of us expected.

Beyond shopping, the most common connectors are for personal productivity and connecting Muse to your other services like email and calendar. This shows the importance of the Muse Secure VM that we've built to provide state-of-the-art privacy and security, and we're looking forward to following up soon with the Muse Confidential VM, which will make it so that even Meta cannot see your content.

[META | FY2026 Q3 | TRANSCRIPT]
Speaker: Susan Li, CFO
Meta One is rolling out gradually with more than 50

features across Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp, including Meta Business Agent and Meta AI, and has surpassed 15 million subscriptions and trials to date. The core experience across our apps and Meta AI will remain free, while subscriptions offer more specialized capabilities and expanded AI usage.

Beyond monetizing engagement across our existing services, we are building new experiences and revenue streams around consumer agents.

Mark highlighted the impressive early momentum with Muse. Users have found many reasons to use Muse with the top 3 categories being shopping, personal productivity and creativity. We are encouraged by the breadth of use cases, with shopping in particular being used by over 25% of Muse weekly actives.

While our near-term priority is to grow adoption and expand Muse's reach, we see multiple paths to monetization, beginning with subscriptions.

We also see a significant opportunity to extend Muse to small businesses. Based on a recent user survey, we estimate that at least 500 million self-identified small businesses use Meta's family of apps to reach customers and generate revenue. Muse could help these businesses acquire customers and operate more efficiently, while helping people complete transactions. Over time, consumer and business agents could connect and transact directly, creating opportunities around paid usage, commerce, and business services.

Alongside growth, we are focused on building sustainable unit economics. Muse's compute intensity means that expanding its user base will require significant investment, and we expect total serving costs to rise. At the same time, we expect to improve compute cost efficiency by more than tenfold over the next year, driven by better utilization of off-peak capacity, more efficient models and inference optimization.

As revenue scales, these efficiency gains give us confidence in our ability to build a highly profitable business over time.

Moving now to our financial outlook.

We expect fourth quarter 2026 total revenue to be in the range of $73-76 billion. Our guidance assumes foreign currency is an approximately 1% headwind to year-over-year total revenue growth, based on current exchange rates.

Turning to the expense and capex outlooks.

We are raising our expense outlook to incorporate the $9.9 billion charge related to legal proceedings recognized in Q3. We now expect full year 2026 total expenses to be in the range of $175-179 billion.

Excluding the Q3 legal charge, we continue to expect 2026 operating income to be above 2025 operating income.

At a segment level, we now expect Reality Labs losses to decline compared to 2025 to a range of $18-19 billion.

We anticipate 2026 capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, to be in the range of $135-145 billion, narrowed from our prior outlook of $130-145 billion.

Speaker: Mark Zuckerberg, CEO
And as our upcoming models get even more advanced, I expect that we’re going to see an increasing rate of improvement in these systems.

Alright, let's talk about the models now. Muse Wonder is state-of-the-art across many dimensions that matter for personal superintelligence. This validates the importance of training models ourselves to deliver the best experience. In addition to Muse, we've also seen that engagement per person in Meta AI has more than doubled since April when we started rolling out our new models.

While Muse Wonder has been our most important release, I've been very pleased with our pace of execution here. In the last few months we've shipped Muse Spark 1.2 and 1.3, Muse Code, two open weights models with Muse Glimmer and Muse Spark Open, and also Muse Voice.

Going forward, with the field advancing quickly, we plan to focus on both pushing the frontier of intelligence and distilling those models into much smaller and more efficient product models that will be optimized for personal agents. My view is that we will be able to build superintelligence through scaling, so we are methodically working our way up the ladder there. We are already working on larger models after Muse Wonder, and they're going to be very impressive and capable. We’re also working on new smaller models that are coming out soon that will deliver Muse Wonder-level intelligence more efficiently.

Moving on, our work on personal superintelligence is now also the focus of Reality Labs. Muse is coming to Meta Glasses starting next month, and that will be an important step towards this. People already love many features of the glasses already -- music, calling, capturing moments,

hearing assistance, and more -- but over time we expect Muse and having your personal superintelligence with you throughout the day will be the most important part of the experience.

Muse is also central to the business model for the glasses. Again, our mission and strategy are to serve everyone here. We believe in putting the power of this technology in everyone's hands. So we have priced our devices not to make a large profit on the hardware, but to build a large software and superintelligence business on top of them over time. Glasses sales continue to grow rapidly, and now with Muse, we expect that paid subscriptions will increase and that this business will begin improving meaningfully from here.

I also shared at Connect that we are changing our approach to virtual reality to only ship new devices when we have major breakthroughs like we had with the Meta VR Glasses this year -- which of course are the first VR experience ever in a pair of glasses. I continue to believe that the path to delivering the holographic experience of bringing together the physical and digital worlds in everyday glasses will come through VR first, but we will pace this aspect of our investment more to focus on delivering personal superintelligence first.

Beyond shopping, the most common connectors are for personal productivity and connecting Muse to your other services like email and calendar. This shows the importance of the Muse Secure VM that we've built to provide state-of-the-art privacy and security, and we're looking forward to following up soon with the Muse Confidential VM, which will make it so that even Meta cannot see your content.

We have also seen that Muse Wonder improves quality, engagement, and retention further, which suggests that as we continue to improve intelligence, Muse will perform better and better over time.

Now that Muse has clear product-market fit, we're entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it. The goals of this next phase play to many of Meta's strengths. We need to do three things: scale the product, grow revenue, and optimize compute costs.

We expect to grow Muse to serve billions of people. This is both our mission and our strategy. It's our mission in that we believe in putting the power of personal superintelligence in everyone's hands. We believe that that is the path to ensuring a positive future for everyone with individual empowerment as the source of prosperity and balance of power as the foundation for safety. On a values level, we believe that delivering this capability widely is the best thing that we can be doing. This is also our strategy, because we think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together. And for those who want Muse to help improve the personalization and quality of their content and ads across Meta, they will be able to connect to those experiences as well.

Just to clarify, the average revenue that I was talking about before is the Family of Apps revenue for our existing Muse users.

[META | FY2026 Q3 | TRANSCRIPT]
Speaker: Susan Li, CFO
Thanks, Doug.

So on your first question about how the agentic ecosystem evolves, I wish I could sort of predict that more perfectly. And I think it will take some time. And again I think it will be a little uneven.

But I definitely think that when I use Muse today it's clear that there are a lot of parts of the experience that would be even better if Muse was able to interact more seamlessly with business agents on the other side.

For example, when -- if Muse has to call a business on my behalf, I think it would be easier for the business if that call was handled by business agents that were representing it. And I think also one of the things that is really distinctive about Muse and one of the things that makes the product

experience so great is the degree of proactivity that it exhibits on my behalf, right?

I can give it a task and Muse is going to go execute against that task for me even as it encounters some obstacles or can't quite find the right thing and needs to chart a new path to helping me look for the thing I want.

And so I think the -- that sort of dimension of proactivity exhibited by either consumer agents or business agents, I think are going to enable more transactions to happen or more activity to happen broadly than happens today where -- when things are -- when more actions are taken, primarily -- when like the latent demand expresses itself versus things where I can have Muse searching for things for me on an ongoing basis, giving me regular updates on things I'm looking for, sending me 10 new books a month.

And agents should be doing similar things for businesses, and I think that creates sort of opportunities, again for a new more proactive sort of framework for what agent-to-agent interactions look like over time.

On your second question which is about 2027, we are quite early in developing our budget and capacity plans for next year.

So we are, I would say at the point where we are both investing -- sorry, evaluating a lot of investment proposals that have attractive return profiles over different time horizons, and we want to figure out how we can fund as many of those as possible within the construct of our overall budget and financial goals.

But it's very dynamic and it's still pretty early. And so we don't have anything more specific or quantitative to share until we get to the Q4 call which is typically when we share guidance for the next year.

Speaker: Mark Zuckerberg, CEO
For business owners who want additional features to use Muse to grow their businesses or for companies that want people to use Muse for work, they will be able to subscribe directly and pay as well.

And for those who want Muse to help improve the personalization and quality of their content and ads across Meta, they will be able to connect to those experiences as well.

Just to clarify, the average revenue that I was talking about before is the Family of Apps revenue for our existing Muse users.

On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years. In the near term, Muse is very compute-intensive to run. But we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale. If compute efficiency continues improving quickly for another few years, which we think is highly likely, then Muse will be highly profitable over multiple years. In the near term, the strength of our core business enables us to scale the Muse network before then. And we believe that we are the best positioned company to pursue this strategy.

One other note on compute economics is that since training is a large fixed cost, now that we have leading models, we want to serve as much high-margin inference demand as possible. That is why we are building the Meta Enterprise Platform, led by CJ Desai. Muse Wonder and even more advanced models that we are training can serve additional high-margin services beyond the Muse network, including our API, Muse Code, and other enterprise services.

A fundamental feature of our business is that we have many good uses for this compute. It is difficult to forecast the exact growth rates for the Muse network, for our enterprise platform, and for how Muse Wonder and beyond will accelerate our core business. But through building out multiple ways to deploy these advanced models, we increase the chances that one or more of them significantly outperforms our expectations. Beyond serving other businesses, we have not yet found the limit of how effectively we can apply compute to accelerating our own core business. We have implemented an eval with Muse Wonder to improve how effectively it can autonomously improve our recommendations and ads systems. And as our upcoming models get even more advanced, I expect that we’re going to see an increasing rate of improvement in these systems.

Alright, let's talk about the models now. Muse Wonder is state-of-the-art across many dimensions that matter for personal superintelligence. This validates the importance of training models ourselves to deliver the best experience. In addition to Muse, we've also seen that engagement per person in Meta AI has more than doubled since April when we started rolling out our new models.
sources.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg, CEO

sources.content:
[META | FY2026 Q3 | TRANSCRIPT]
Speaker: Mark Zuckerberg, CEO
That's why I mentioned that we launched Muse first on Muse Spark, and that's what is currently the default across the free tier. And we rolled out Muse Wonder, and people can access that in the paid tier today. And we know that it performs a

lot better, so we're working on getting a more efficient version of Muse Wonder that we'll be able to roll out more broadly.

But you can imagine just as we iterate forward in two, three models into the future, when you have significantly higher intelligence and capability to solve many more problems for people and the ability to deliver that at a much more affordable price point, I think that that's going to just unlock a lot more value to people. So we're very excited about that.

Transitioning to talking about the enterprise piece because I think these two pieces, there is some connection here in that the main enterprise offering in the near term is going to be the model API and Muse Code. And we have business agents that we've been scaling for a while, and each of those three things is growing quite quickly. So we're excited about that.

Over time we would like to make it so that we have a whole kind of business network of Muse agents as well.

There's the business agent which we've talked about on previous earnings calls for businesses to help out with sales and customer support.

But what we see is a lot of people are actually using Muse today to help run especially small businesses. And we think that there's both an opportunity to help create an agent that people use to really enable them to automate and do a lot of the parts of spinning up a small business that are just kind of difficult and time consuming but aren't the core thing that a person is trying to do.

So we think that's a big deal. And then making a version of Muse that people can bring into different corporate environments and work there, we think is going to be a big deal.

And then beyond that, building what I refer to as the Muse network which is making it so that Muse is not just a kind of single player game where you have your Muse but making it so that your Muses can work with your friends and your families. And if you want to buy something, it's not just navigating to that business' website. It's talking to their agent. I think that getting that all to work well together is going to unlock tremendous value at scale.

So I'm very excited about all of that. I think the enterprise use is going to be a big part of it, but it's also going to kind of have this very valuable boost in the utility for consumers, too. So I'm very excited about both of those.
sources.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg, CEO

sources.content:
[META | FY2026 Q3 | TRANSCRIPT]
Speaker: Susan Li, CFO
Yes. I would add to that, and I will also answer your second question and just say I think agents are going to be an important part of how reality evolves, and I think everyone is going to have to adapt to what that means, the new age of agentic commerce.

We obviously have had a lot of businesses we're very excited to partner with us. There are also businesses that are understandably focused on protecting customer relationships. And we expect the market, I think ultimately to evolve away from agents attempting to navigate every digital experience like a human.

And I think over the long run, this will move towards more permissioned, structured interactions, and that will include authenticated APIs, approved agent partnerships or direct communications between the consumer's personal agent and a business' own agent.

And we're helping establish the standards needed to support that model. Earlier this month, we previewed the Personal Agent Protocol, an open standard across Muse and Meta business agents that we are developing with industry partners like Sierra, Walmart, Stripe, Shopify, et cetera. The protocol is intended to define how a consumer's personal agent can interact securely and reliably with the business' agent and preserve appropriate controls for both the business and customers.

So again I think adoption will likely be uneven and will take time and in the near term, we expect any experience -- many experiences will remain AI assisted rather than fully autonomous.

But as trusted integrations develop and agents demonstrate that they can generate incremental value and demand and operate safely, we expect that more and more businesses will be excited to participate.

Your second question was about the announcement of the new class of shares.

So I should say we created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders.

We believe this share class will maintain our founder-led structure. It will expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we're seeing across every part of our business driven by AI.

We don't have any specific financing plans to announce at this time but we thought it was prudent to establish the appropriate capital structure framework to ensure that we have access to a diverse pool of funding sources.
sources.speaker: Susan Li, CFO

sources.content:
[META | FY2026 Q3 | TRANSCRIPT]
Speaker: Mark Zuckerberg, CEO
My guess I think that we are going to work on monetization somewhat sooner on this than our normal playbook for a couple of reasons.

One is just the size of the numbers that we're talking about in terms of both the costs and the opportunity, I think make it kind of important to make progress on that in order to be able to scale it. The other is just that such a large part of what people are doing is commerce. And to your question, that does include travel, too, I think we might consider travel a different case, but travel is actually one of the other top use cases for Muse, is basically people planning

that out and planning different kinds of things that they would get than they might get through our Family of Apps.

So I think that this is going to be an important thing for us to work on to deliver the consumer value that people want, and in doing so, I think we will be able to build a model where we get a percent of the value that we are helping to create for people.

So I think that that's going to be -- it's going to be very important to kind of get the math on all of this to work out so that way we can continue the compute build-out that we want to build in order to get this to reach everyone at scale.

And in addition to everything that Susan said in response to the last answer, I would also just add that like we just see this trend that year-over-year, I just expect that we will be able to deliver the same intelligence that we have now in Muse Wonder or, frankly, any of the current frontier models at a fraction of the cost in a smaller model a year from today.

So to the extent that that represents some kind of baseline level that people seem to -- that kind of is sufficient for product market fit for Muse, I think that we will just continue through continued model development, make progress on that efficiency. The thing that is -- and of course less clear is that I don't think in a year from now most people are going to want to use the current model level of intelligence because that's also going to make progress.

So I think we're going to need to work on all of these things, both the revenue pieces of it and scaling the different aspects of that as well as progressing on the model development and all the efficiency in order to be able to both fund and support the compute build-out and reach billions of people which, again we want to get to that as soon as possible.

Part of the reason why we're not just charging everyone upfront to use this is we want to establish this Muse network, and we think that it's going to be more valuable for people at scale when there are a lot of people and businesses using Muse so that way they can collaborate and work together.

Yes. I think I can talk about both of those, and then Susan can jump in with anything else. All right.

So right now for Muse, we are -- and one of the things I pointed out is we have more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada who have set it up, but I think one of the biggest constraints so far is that because this is a compute- intensive service to run, we have not launched it globally yet. That's partially because of wanting to optimize it for each place, and there's some work around connectors for that. But it's partially that we want to make sure that we do this efficiently.

So I mean there's pros and cons there. The pro, of course is that, that just makes it even more impressive that you have 10 million people using it and signing up to use it in the first six weeks because those are all kind of Americans and Canadians in a small number of markets.

So if you actually did roll it out more broadly, then you would expect that number to be significantly larger than what we're seeing today.

But then on the flip side, we actually have to go do the work to bring the efficiency in line to make that make sense.

And so that's a big part of it that we need to do. We -- the compute efficiency work is going to be important on this also because we want to make sure that we've built enough compute to be able to serve what we think is going to be 1 billion plus people if we can achieve certain compute efficiency targets, but we obviously have a lot of work to do there as well. And that will be one of the limiting factors over the next year.

We want to build out the business around it. So I talked about that. And I think doing that in tandem with bringing down the compute -- or increasing the compute efficiency is going to be important for getting this to work from a business perspective which I'm optimistic about, but I think that that's one of the things that we need to do.

And then there's just continuing to increase the value in the product which I think we will largely do by continuing to develop new models. That's why I mentioned that we launched Muse first on Muse Spark, and that's what is currently the default across the free tier. And we rolled out Muse Wonder, and people can access that in the paid tier today. And we know that it performs a

lot better, so we're working on getting a more efficient version of Muse Wonder that we'll be able to roll out more broadly.

[META | FY2026 Q3 | TRANSCRIPT]
Speaker: Susan Li, CFO
Thanks, Mark. Your second question was around Muse for small business.

So we launched that which you can think of as an expansion for Muse in late September and rather than a separate product, it's kind of a new -- a set of new skills and connectors inside the existing Muse app aimed at helping SMB owners run operations, find new customers.

It connects to a business', for example, Instagram account, analytics or Facebook pages or Meta ad accounts in a few clicks, along with dozens of third-party connectors that businesses already run on like Shopify, QuickBooks, Canva, et cetera. It already understands what businesses sell. Its brand voice, what customers are asking for.

And Muse can take actions including analyze ad and content performance, draft campaigns, customer responses, flag issues, and we are actively listening to our SMB users to understand what their top use cases are.

We are seeing them use it for ads optimization, for direct message organizing, use it to expand their sales footprint to keep their website current based on things like inventory and new products to deal with employee load balancing.

So we're pretty closely following how businesses use Muse to make sure that we are being thoughtful about new features that we release in Muse to make it maximally useful and productive for SMBs.

I'd also say we have unique touch points to, again I mentioned in my opening remarks, 500 million self-identified small businesses. And we think that many of the investments that we make in consumer products are going to carry over to help power those businesses also.

We have multiple excellent channels to surface those opportunities to small businesses globally.

So this is a place where we feel like we have an existing extremely strong platform, and we're very excited about it. And we also believe the transition to AI has broadly unlocked enterprise as a new opportunity for us as well.

[META | FY2026 Q3 | TRANSCRIPT]
Speaker: Susan Li, CFO
We estimate that advertisers who adopted its recommendations drove almost 5% more conversions at the same cost per conversion and increased their advertising investment by 9% compared with similar non-adopters. We are rolling out additional capabilities, including creative insights, stronger business context and more agentic actions. These features will allow marketers to plan, create and optimize campaigns, as well as schedule tasks and alerts, through a conversational experience with approvals and previews that keep them in control.

I’ll share one example of how Meta AI business assistant is empowering our advertisers. Simply Organic Maple, a family-run maple syrup producer in Vermont, used Meta AI business assistant to improve its campaign messaging. After the business assistant recommended testing longer, more descriptive advertising copy, the business saw a 57% increase in purchases and a 36% reduction in cost per purchase. Its strongest revised ad delivered a 3x return on ad spend, a 52% improvement from the original.

Adoption of our generative AI ad creative tools also continues to scale. In Q3, nearly 10 million advertisers used at least one of these tools. Advertiser adoption of our video generation features grew 25% quarter-over-quarter, driven in part by ready-made videos that reduce generation time to just a few seconds from a single image upload.

We're also expanding the opportunity at the intersection of creators and advertising.

Partnership Ads, which allow advertisers to run ads with creators, brands and other businesses, continued to scale rapidly in Q3. Our partnership ads product grew over 97% year-over-year and surpassed $15 billion in annual revenue run-rate.

In Q3, we also completed the global rollout of Creator Marketing Hub to all advertisers, bringing creator discovery, content organization and partnership ad activation into one place, with more than 10 million creators now discoverable. We are integrating Meta AI Business Assistant into the Hub so advertisers can conversationally search for creators, identify content to use in partnership ads and get guidance across their creator marketing workflows.

Outside of ads, we are also building out additional ways to monetize engagement across our ecosystem.

In September, we announced the global expansion of Meta One, our unified subscription service for consumers, creators and businesses. Meta One is rolling out gradually with more than 50

features across Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp, including Meta Business Agent and Meta AI, and has surpassed 15 million subscriptions and trials to date. The core experience across our apps and Meta AI will remain free, while subscriptions offer more specialized capabilities and expanded AI usage.

Beyond monetizing engagement across our existing services, we are building new experiences and revenue streams around consumer agents.

Section: Legal and Related Matters
We filed a petition for a writ of certiorari with the U.S. Supreme Court on October 2, 2024, which was denied. We then moved to compel arbitration, which the district court denied. We appealed the denial of our motion to compel arbitration to the Ninth Circuit on December 3, 2025. The matter is stayed in district court pending resolution of our appeal.

Beginning on July 7, 2023, multiple cases, including putative class actions, were filed against us in the United States and elsewhere, alleging that we improperly acquired, distributed, and used various copyrighted materials and/or other types of data to train our artificial intelligence models and seeking unspecified damages and injunctive relief. In the United States, statutory damages for copyright liability are calculated on a per work basis, which may result in substantial damages, particularly given the large volumes of data required to train AI models. The cases in the United States, which were filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California (Kadrey, et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., Chabon, et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc. and Farnsworth v. Meta Platforms, Inc.) and U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York (Huckabee, et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc. et al., which was subsequently transferred to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California), have been consolidated into Kadrey, et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc. Motions for summary judgment were heard in this case on May 1, 2025, including on the issue of the applicability of the fair use defense to use of copyrighted books for generative AI model training. On June 25, 2025, the court granted our motion for summary judgment on fair use as to the named plaintiffs in the case. The parties will proceed to brief the remaining claims of copyright infringement and contributory infringement related to alleged distribution of books to third parties during the downloading process. The court is scheduled to hear summary judgment motions on February 25, 2027. Beginning in November 2025, additional cases with similar claims were filed against us in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California and the Southern District of New York (Entrepreneur Media v. Meta Platforms, Inc., Carreyrou et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., TED Entertainment, Inc. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., Chicken Soup for the Soul LLC v. Meta Platforms, Inc., Beaulier v. Meta Platforms, Inc., Cognella, Inc. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., Elsevier Inc. et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc. et al., Hobbs et al. v. Meta

[META | FY2026 Q3 | TRANSCRIPT]
Speaker: Mark Zuckerberg, CEO
I also shared at Connect that we are changing our approach to virtual reality to only ship new devices when we have major breakthroughs like we had with the Meta VR Glasses this year -- which of course are the first VR experience ever in a pair of glasses. I continue to believe that the path to delivering the holographic experience of bringing together the physical and digital worlds in everyday glasses will come through VR first, but we will pace this aspect of our investment more to focus on delivering personal superintelligence first.

So with these factors combined, we expect that the P&L of Reality Labs to improve from here, with operating loss coming down to around $15B next year and trending towards profitability from there.

Before we conclude, I want to spend a moment on the sheer velocity that we're seeing. An important part of our approach has always been to move fast so we can learn quickly and serve people better at scale. But recently things have accelerated. In the last year, we shipped Edits and it has already passed 50 million actives. New apps like Forum and Seller were built by small teams and are scaling quickly to serve power users. Muse went from an idea on a whiteboard to a successful product in just about eight months. And we're about to ship Muse Charm, which will have gone from concept to a hardware device in people's pockets in less than a year.

I'm proud of what we're building. People have all kinds of different opinions about the future, but at Meta we believe that the future is for everyone and that putting power in people's hands is how we get there. I think that this matters. There needs to be a company out there that represents these ideas. But this isn't just about ideas; it's also about execution. So I'm grateful for everyone who is working so hard to deliver all of this to billions of people around the world. And as always, thank you to everyone who is on this journey with us. And now here's Susan.

Alphabet Announces Third Quarter 2026 Results

MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif. – October 28, 2026 – Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOG, GOOGL) today announced financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

•Consolidated Alphabet revenues increased 25% to $127.6 billion, reflecting strong performance across the business and our 13th consecutive quarter of double-digit revenue growth.

•Google Services revenues increased 11% to $96.3 billion, led by 12% growth in Google Search & other with the year-over-year Search query growth rate the highest it has been in the last five years.

•Google Cloud delivered record growth as revenues increased 103% to $30.7 billion, led by strong growth in Google Cloud Platform (GCP) across enterprise AI infrastructure and enterprise AI solutions, as well as core GCP services. TPU systems sales were also a meaningful contributor to revenue growth.

•Consolidated Alphabet operating income increased 30% and operating margin was 31.8%.

•Net income available to common stockholders was $26.2 billion and EPS was $2.12.

Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google and Alphabet, said:

“We had a strong quarter and are now on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate. Our deep full stack approach is driving momentum across the business, with Alphabet revenues growing 25% year-over year.

Our AI investments are driving overall Search query growth, including commercial queries. In fact, our year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it’s been in the last five years.

Google Cloud revenues grew 103%, powered by huge demand for our AI infrastructure and AI solutions. We’re also seeing strong demand for our TPU systems across a wide range of customers.

Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon are now leading at the frontier. Overall, our first-party model APIs are now processing nearly 32 billion tokens per minute, more than four times what we processed a year ago.

On top of that, the Gemini app has reached one billion users—making it the fastest-growing product in Google’s history—and we surpassed 150 million YouTube Music and Premium subscribers globally, including trials.

We’re excited by the range of big opportunities ahead of us.”

Section: 2026 Q3 Earnings Call
Speaker: Anat Ashkenazi, SVP and CFO, Alphabet and Google
Thank you, Thomas.

My comments will focus on year-over-year comparisons for the third quarter, unless I state otherwise.

I will start with the results at the Alphabet level and will then cover our segment results. I'll end with some commentary and our outlook for the fourth quarter and full year 2026.

We had a strong third quarter, delivering our thirteenth consecutive quarter of double-digit revenue growth.

Consolidated revenues were $127.6 billion, up 25% in both reported and constant currency.

Total cost of revenue was $51.4 billion, up 24%. TAC was $16.4 billion, up 10%.

Other Cost of Revenues was $35.1 billion, up 32%, driven by hardware costs primarily related to the sales of TPU systems, increase in depreciation, content acquisition costs, and technical infrastructure operations costs.

Total operating expenses were up 20% to $35.6 billion.

R&D expenses increased by 36%, driven by compensation, primarily for investment in AI talent as well as depreciation.

Sales and Marketing expenses were up 22%, due to investments in Gemini and compensation.

And G&A expenses decreased 17%, primarily due to lapping of higher legal expenses that occurred in Q3 last year, partially offset by current year legal charges.

Operating income increased 30% to $40.6 billion, and operating margin was 31.8%.

Other income and expenses was negative $8.2 billion, due primarily to unrealized loss from our investment in SpaceX from a decline in its stock price in the third quarter.

Net income and earnings per share decreased due to the decline in OI&E.

We generated strong operating cash flow of $42.3 billion in the third quarter and $179.6 billion for the trailing 12 months.

Operating cash flow was negatively impacted by the buildup of inventory for TPU system sales, as well as a $5.2 billion cash payment for a 2018 EC fine following the conclusion of the appeal process.

CapEx was $51.4 billion in the third quarter with the vast majority of the spend in technical infrastructure to support our investments in AI. Approximately 65% of our investments in technical infrastructure in Q3 was related to servers and networking equipment, which generally have useful lives of six years. The remaining 35% was for data centers, which have useful lives of seven to 40 years.

We had negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, driven by our investments in CapEx. Free cash flow in the third quarter was also affected by the aforementioned inventory bill to support TPU system sales and payment of the EC fine.

Free cash flow was $19.7 billion for the trailing 12 months.

Section: Note 12. Net Income Per Common Share
We compute net income per common share of Class A, Class B, and Class C stock using the two-class method. Basic net income per common share is computed using the weighted-average number of shares outstanding during the period. Diluted net income per common share is computed using the weighted-average number of shares and the effect of potentially dilutive securities outstanding during the period. Potentially dilutive securities consist of restricted stock units (RSUs), other contingently issuable shares, and mandatory convertible preferred stock. The dilutive effect of outstanding RSUs and other contingently issuable shares is reflected in diluted earnings per common share pursuant to the treasury stock method. The dilutive effect of mandatory convertible preferred shares is reflected in diluted earnings per common share pursuant to the if-converted method. The computation of the diluted net income per common share of Class A stock assumes the conversion of Class B stock, while the diluted net income per common share of Class B stock does not assume the conversion of those shares.

Net income available to common stockholders is calculated by adjusting net income to deduct declared and accrued dividends on the mandatory convertible preferred stock.

In accordance with our certificate of incorporation, the rights, including the liquidation and dividend rights, of the holders of our Class A, Class B, and Class C stock are identical, except with respect to voting. Furthermore, there are a number of safeguards built into our certificate of incorporation, as well as Delaware law, which preclude our Board of Directors from declaring or paying unequal per share dividends on our Class A, Class B, and Class C stock. Specifically, Delaware law provides that amendments to our certificate of incorporation which would have the effect of adversely altering the rights, powers, or preferences of a given class of stock must be approved by the class of stock adversely affected by the proposed amendment. In addition, our certificate of incorporation provides that before any such amendment may be put to a stockholder vote, it must be approved by the unanimous consent of our Board of Directors.

Immaterial differences in net income per common share across our Class A, Class B, and Class C shares may arise due to the allocation of distributed earnings, which is based on the holders as of the record date, compared with the allocation of undistributed earnings and number of shares, which is based on the weighted-average shares outstanding over the periods.

Unless earlier converted, each outstanding share will automatically convert on the mandatory conversion date, which is on or about May 15, 2029. The conversion rate for each share of our Series A mandatory convertible preferred stock will be between 2.2520 and 2.8160 shares of Class A stock, and Series B mandatory convertible preferred stock will convert into between 2.2740 and 2.8420 shares of Class C stock, depending on the applicable market value of our Class A and Class C stock upon conversion and subject to certain anti-dilution adjustments. The applicable market value will be determined based on the average volume-weighted average price per share over the 20 consecutive trading day final averaging period ending immediately prior to the mandatory conversion date.

If a fundamental change occurs on or prior to May 15, 2029, holders of mandatory convertible preferred stock will automatically convert into Class A or Class C shares, as applicable, at a special fundamental change conversion rate and, under certain circumstances, receive a fundamental change dividend make-whole amount. Other than during a fundamental change conversion period, at any time prior to May 15, 2029, holders may elect to convert at the minimum conversion rate, subject to certain anti-dilution and other adjustments.

question: How did Meta's 2026 capital expenditure outlook change over the last four quarters?
answer:
Here is the capital expenditure outlook for Meta over the last four quarters of 2026:

**FY2026 Q1**
- Anticipated capital expenditures: $115-135 billion [1][2].

**FY2026 Q2**
- Revised anticipated capital expenditures: $125-145 billion, increased from the previous range due to higher component pricing and additional data center costs [2][3].

**FY2026 Q3**
- Further revised anticipated capital expenditures: $130-145 billion, narrowed from the previous outlook [3][4].

**FY2026 Q4**
- Latest anticipated capital expenditures: $135-145 billion, narrowed from the previous outlook [4][8].

In summary, the capital expenditure outlook increased from a range of $115-135 billion in Q1 to a range of $135-145 billion by Q4, reflecting ongoing investments in infrastructure and technology.

More broadly, as we invest in infrastructure to meet our business needs, we continue to prioritize maintaining long-term flexibility so we can adapt to how the market develops. We’re doing so in several ways, including changing how we develop data center sites, establishing strategic partnerships, contracting cloud capacity, and establishing new ownership structures for some of our large data center sites.

We have a strong net cash balance and expect our business will continue to generate sufficient cash to fund our infrastructure investments in 2026, which is reflected in our expectations. Nonetheless, we will continue to look for opportunities to periodically supplement our strong operating cash flow with prudent amounts of cost-efficient external financing, which may lead us to eventually maintain a positive net debt balance.

Moving to our financial outlook.

We expect first quarter 2026 total revenue to be in the range of $53.5-56.5 billion. Our guidance assumes foreign currency is an approximately 4% tailwind to year-over-year total revenue growth, based on current exchange rates.

Turning to the expense and capex outlooks.

We expect full year 2026 total expenses to be in the range of $162-169 billion.

The majority of expense growth will be driven by infrastructure costs, which includes third party cloud spend, higher depreciation, and higher infrastructure operating expenses.

The second-largest contributor to total expense growth is employee compensation, driven by investments in technical talent. This includes 2026 hires to support our priority areas, particularly AI, as well as a full year of expenses from 2025 hires.

At a segment level, we expect expense growth to be driven by the Family of Apps, with Reality Labs operating losses remaining similar to 2025 levels.

We anticipate 2026 capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, to be in the range of $115-135 billion, with year-over-year growth driven by increased investment to support our Meta Superintelligence Labs efforts and core business.

Despite the meaningful step up in infrastructure investment, in 2026 we expect to deliver operating income that is above 2025 operating income.

Absent any changes to our tax landscape, we expect our full year 2026 tax rate to be 13-16%.

Finally, we recently aligned with the European Commission on further changes to our Less Personalized Ads offering, which we will begin rolling out this quarter. However, we continue to monitor legal and regulatory headwinds in the EU and the US that could significantly impact our business and financial results. For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth-related issues and have a number of trials scheduled for this year in the US, which may ultimately result in a material loss.

Speaker: Susan Li, CFO
Last month, we rolled out our affiliate partnerships offering on Facebook to more test partners, so creators can tag products from participating retailers on their posts and earn a commission when someone makes a purchase. We have also started testing similar experiences on Instagram.

We see a real opportunity to help people more easily discover and buy products within our services, particularly as we incorporate AI deeply across our platforms.

Next, I would like to discuss our approach to capital allocation.

Compute is becoming increasingly important as it determines the quality of the services we can provide, including powering more capable models and delivering innovative new products. It is also becoming more critical to how we work at Meta, as we are entering a world where employees are managing agents to help them generate new ideas, run experiments, execute tasks, and build products.

We are investing aggressively to meet our infrastructure needs and ensure we maximize our strategic flexibility over the coming years. This includes substantially expanding our own data center footprint and striking deals throughout the supply chain to secure necessary components for future capacity. We are also signing cloud deals that will come online over the course of this year and 2027, allowing us to scale more quickly. These multi-year cloud deals and our

infrastructure purchase agreements drove a $107 billion step up in our contractual commitments this quarter.

Our investments will support our training needs for future models, and most importantly, provide us the inference capacity necessary to deliver personal and business agents to billions of people around the world, along with several other AI product experiences we’re developing.

As we grow our infrastructure spend, we remain committed to operating efficiently, and we recently shared internally that we plan to reduce the size of our employee base in May. We believe a leaner operating model will allow us to move more quickly while also helping to offset the substantial investments we’re making.

Moving to our financial outlook.

We expect second quarter 2026 total revenue to be in the range of $58-61 billion. Our guidance assumes foreign currency is an approximately 2% tailwind to year-over-year total revenue growth, based on current exchange rates.

Turning to the expense and capex outlooks.

We expect full year 2026 total expenses to be in the range of $162-169 billion, unchanged from our prior outlook.

We continue to expect to deliver operating income this year that is above 2025 operating income.

We anticipate 2026 capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, to be in the range of $125-145 billion, increased from our prior range of $115-135 billion. This reflects our expectations for higher component pricing this year and, to a lesser extent, additional data center costs to support future year capacity.

Absent any changes to our tax landscape, we expect our tax rate for the remaining quarters of 2026 to be between 13-16%.

Speaker: Susan Li, CFO
Meta One is rolling out gradually with more than 50

features across Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp, including Meta Business Agent and Meta AI, and has surpassed 15 million subscriptions and trials to date. The core experience across our apps and Meta AI will remain free, while subscriptions offer more specialized capabilities and expanded AI usage.

Beyond monetizing engagement across our existing services, we are building new experiences and revenue streams around consumer agents.

Mark highlighted the impressive early momentum with Muse. Users have found many reasons to use Muse with the top 3 categories being shopping, personal productivity and creativity. We are encouraged by the breadth of use cases, with shopping in particular being used by over 25% of Muse weekly actives.

While our near-term priority is to grow adoption and expand Muse's reach, we see multiple paths to monetization, beginning with subscriptions.

We also see a significant opportunity to extend Muse to small businesses. Based on a recent user survey, we estimate that at least 500 million self-identified small businesses use Meta's family of apps to reach customers and generate revenue. Muse could help these businesses acquire customers and operate more efficiently, while helping people complete transactions. Over time, consumer and business agents could connect and transact directly, creating opportunities around paid usage, commerce, and business services.

Alongside growth, we are focused on building sustainable unit economics. Muse's compute intensity means that expanding its user base will require significant investment, and we expect total serving costs to rise. At the same time, we expect to improve compute cost efficiency by more than tenfold over the next year, driven by better utilization of off-peak capacity, more efficient models and inference optimization.

As revenue scales, these efficiency gains give us confidence in our ability to build a highly profitable business over time.

Moving now to our financial outlook.

We expect fourth quarter 2026 total revenue to be in the range of $73-76 billion. Our guidance assumes foreign currency is an approximately 1% headwind to year-over-year total revenue growth, based on current exchange rates.

Turning to the expense and capex outlooks.

We are raising our expense outlook to incorporate the $9.9 billion charge related to legal proceedings recognized in Q3. We now expect full year 2026 total expenses to be in the range of $175-179 billion.

Excluding the Q3 legal charge, we continue to expect 2026 operating income to be above 2025 operating income.

At a segment level, we now expect Reality Labs losses to decline compared to 2025 to a range of $18-19 billion.

We anticipate 2026 capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, to be in the range of $135-145 billion, narrowed from our prior outlook of $130-145 billion.

Section: Reality Labs Products
Many of our Reality Labs investments are directed toward long-term, cutting edge research and development for products that are not on the market today and may only be fully realized in the next decade. This includes exploring innovations in AI and hardware to help build next-generation interfaces. In the near term, we are continuing to develop products and experiences that help people feel connected, anytime, anywhere.

Our current product offerings in VR include our Meta Quest devices, as well as software and content available through the Meta Horizon Store, which enable a range of social experiences that allow people to defy physical distance while engaging in gaming, fitness, entertainment, and more. To drive greater adoption and acceptance of VR we have introduced passthrough capabilities, which allow users to experience the immersion and presence of VR while still being grounded in the physical world, through our Meta Quest devices.

Our wearables efforts include our AI glasses and long-term AR initiatives. Our current AI glasses include the Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta glasses, which feature Meta AI, our advanced conversational assistant, as well as other features such as hands-free interaction. As we continue our long-term efforts to bring AR glasses to market, in 2024 we also unveiled our Orion prototype, a pair of true AR glasses that overlay content on top of the physical world. It does this with an industry-leading field of view and in glasses form factor for comfortable wear. In 2025, we introduced Meta Ray-Ban Display, which combines our AI glasses with an integrated display built into the lens. It comes with the Meta Neural Band, which is a wrist-worn wearable device that uses electromyography to let people control their AI glasses using neuromuscular signals.

In general, our Reality Labs efforts include shorter-term projects developing specific products and services to go to market, as well as longer-term research and development projects. All of these investments are part of our long-term initiative to help build the next computing platform. In 2026, we expect to spend approximately 70% of our Reality Labs operating expenses on our wearables initiatives, and the remaining 30% on our VR and Horizon initiatives. We apply significant judgment in estimating this expense breakdown as there are certain shared costs across product lines, and our expectations are subject to change, including as the next computing platform and our business strategies evolve. In particular, we regularly evaluate our product roadmaps and make significant changes as our understanding of the technological challenges and market landscape and our product ideas and designs evolve.

[META | FY2026 Q3 | TRANSCRIPT]
Speaker: Susan Li, CFO
We estimate that advertisers who adopted its recommendations drove almost 5% more conversions at the same cost per conversion and increased their advertising investment by 9% compared with similar non-adopters. We are rolling out additional capabilities, including creative insights, stronger business context and more agentic actions. These features will allow marketers to plan, create and optimize campaigns, as well as schedule tasks and alerts, through a conversational experience with approvals and previews that keep them in control.

I’ll share one example of how Meta AI business assistant is empowering our advertisers. Simply Organic Maple, a family-run maple syrup producer in Vermont, used Meta AI business assistant to improve its campaign messaging. After the business assistant recommended testing longer, more descriptive advertising copy, the business saw a 57% increase in purchases and a 36% reduction in cost per purchase. Its strongest revised ad delivered a 3x return on ad spend, a 52% improvement from the original.

Adoption of our generative AI ad creative tools also continues to scale. In Q3, nearly 10 million advertisers used at least one of these tools. Advertiser adoption of our video generation features grew 25% quarter-over-quarter, driven in part by ready-made videos that reduce generation time to just a few seconds from a single image upload.

We're also expanding the opportunity at the intersection of creators and advertising.

Partnership Ads, which allow advertisers to run ads with creators, brands and other businesses, continued to scale rapidly in Q3. Our partnership ads product grew over 97% year-over-year and surpassed $15 billion in annual revenue run-rate.

In Q3, we also completed the global rollout of Creator Marketing Hub to all advertisers, bringing creator discovery, content organization and partnership ad activation into one place, with more than 10 million creators now discoverable. We are integrating Meta AI Business Assistant into the Hub so advertisers can conversationally search for creators, identify content to use in partnership ads and get guidance across their creator marketing workflows.

Outside of ads, we are also building out additional ways to monetize engagement across our ecosystem.

In September, we announced the global expansion of Meta One, our unified subscription service for consumers, creators and businesses. Meta One is rolling out gradually with more than 50

features across Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp, including Meta Business Agent and Meta AI, and has surpassed 15 million subscriptions and trials to date. The core experience across our apps and Meta AI will remain free, while subscriptions offer more specialized capabilities and expanded AI usage.

Beyond monetizing engagement across our existing services, we are building new experiences and revenue streams around consumer agents.
